title: Everything that breathes (Psalm 150)
hook: the book ends: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD"
carry: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, psalms for the sick, and a community reading the whole book for one person. Your line was something you can hold, together. Did you reach out to someone unwell? Today, the last psalm of all. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

Think about how a great concert ends. Not quietly. The band brings everything in at once. Drums, horns, guitars, the crowd singing along, the lights all on. The last song is the one where nobody holds anything back. The Book of Psalms ends the same way. After a hundred and forty-nine songs of joy and grief, fear and hope, exile and homecoming, the very last psalm is pure, loud, everything-at-once praise. And its final line is about something you're doing right now. Breathing.
screen: `THE LAST SONG OF THE CONCERT.` → `EVERYTHING AT ONCE.` → `THE LAST LINE: BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Psalm one fifty is short, only six verses, and almost every line starts the same way: hallelu, praise. Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him for His mighty acts. And then the instruments pour in: praise Him with the blast of the shofar, with harp and lyre, with drum and dance, with strings and pipe, with loud cymbals, with crashing cymbals. It's the whole orchestra of ancient Israel, all at once. And then, the last line of the whole book: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Hallelujah. After all the instruments, the final one is breath. Not only priests or Levites or musicians. Every thing that breathes. Every person, every animal, anyone who can draw air. Jews say this psalm every morning, near the end of the psalms of praise that open the service, and many repeat that last line twice, to mark the end. The rabbis noticed something in the Hebrew. The word for breath, neshamah, is also the word for soul. And a midrash plays on it: read neshamah as neshimah, a single breath, and it says, for every single breath you take, praise God. Not once a day. Every breath. And so the Book of Psalms, and our two weeks of psalms, ends with breath. We began with a tree by the water, then the stars, the shepherd, the mountain, the open hand, a song for each day, Hallel, and Shabbat. This week: the rivers of Babylon, the depths, the mountains, Elul, sowing in tears, refuah shlemah, and now, everything that breathes.
screen: `HALLELU: PRAISE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SHOFAR, HARP, DRUM, CYMBALS.` · `THE LAST INSTRUMENT IS BREATH.` · `NESHAMAH: BREATH AND SOUL.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe, and praise. Settle. Close your eyes if you like. Take one slow breath in, and one slow breath out. That breath is the last instrument of the Book of Psalms. Now keep breathing, and with each breath out, let one small thanks go with it. For the air. For your body. For someone you love. For this day. You don't need words. The breath can carry it. If you pray, you can say the last line: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. The bell holds the time.
Neshamah. Breath, and soul — the last line of the Book of Psalms calls on everything that has it to praise the Lord, every single breath.
Your line: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. Today, three times, stop and notice one breath, and let it be a thank-you. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Psalm 150 is said every morning as the last of the psalms of praise (Pesukei de-Zimra), and many repeat its final verse to mark the end of the Book of Psalms.

fork.setup: the Book of Psalms has named shofar, harp, lyre, drum, pipe and cymbals. what's the final instrument?
fork.reveal: let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. after the whole orchestra, the last instrument is breath.

original.note: Hebrew: let everything that breathes praise Yah, the last line of Psalms.

trapdoor: what you thought: a loud hymn with instruments.
what it means: the whole book ends by handing praise to every breathing thing.
what a scholar hears: Genesis Rabbah 14:9 reads neshamah (soul, breath) as neshimah (a single breath), and the psalm serves as a closing doxology for the entire five-book collection.
